A samovar is a large, decorated metal container designed specifically to heat water and keep it hot for a long time. Think of it as a self-contained hot-water station — an elegant, ornate appliance built for one dedicated purpose: supplying a continuous stream of steaming-hot water, almost always for making tea.

It is not a teapot. A teapot brews the tea. A samovar only heats and stores the water.

A samovar is immediately recognizable. It is typically a tall, urn-shaped object, often beautifully crafted from brass, copper, bronze, or silver, and frequently polished to a gleaming shine. It stands on small decorative legs and has:

  • A wide, rounded body that holds the water
  • A vertical tube or chimney running through the center (this is what does the heating)
  • A small tap or spigot near the base, through which you draw hot water
  • A lid on top with a small circular platform, just the right size to rest a small teapot

This combination — the graceful metallic shape, the ornate engravings, the tiny teapot perched on top — gives a samovar a very distinctive, almost ceremonial appearance.

Traditionally, the central tube was filled with burning charcoal, wood chips, or even dried pine cones. This tube acts like a chimney: heat travels up through it, warming all the water surrounding it in the body of the vessel. The water gets hot quickly and stays hot for hours.

Modern samovars — still common in homes today — use electricity instead of charcoal, but the design and function are essentially the same.

When you want hot water, you simply open the small tap at the base and let it pour out. No boiling a fresh kettle every time. The samovar is always ready.
How it is used for tea

The samovar is central to a specific style of tea preparation, especially in Russian culture.

Here is how it works:

  1. A small teapot — called a chainik (чайник) in Russian — is used to brew a very small amount of extremely strong, concentrated tea. This concentrate is called zavarka.
  2. This small teapot is placed on the platform on top of the samovar, keeping the concentrate warm using the heat rising from the vessel below.
  3. When someone wants tea, they pour a small splash of the strong concentrate into their cup, then fill the rest of the cup with hot water drawn from the samovar's tap.
  4. The ratio of concentrate to water is adjusted based on personal preference — a little concentrate for mild tea, more for strong tea.

This method means everyone at the table gets tea exactly as strong as they like it, and the samovar keeps things going for hours without anyone needing to reheat anything.

In Russia, the samovar is far more than a kitchen appliance. It is a cultural institution.

For centuries, the samovar was the centerpiece of Russian family life. Gathering around the samovar was the equivalent of gathering around a fireplace — it signaled warmth, hospitality, and togetherness. Guests were always welcomed with tea from the samovar. Family conversations happened around it. It was the social heart of the home.

Samovars were also status symbols. A wealthy family would own an elaborately engraved silver samovar. Poorer families might have a simple copper one. But nearly every Russian household had one. The city of Tula, south of Moscow, became so famous for manufacturing samovars that it became a part of Russian cultural identity — there is even a Russian saying that essentially means "don't bring coals to Newcastle" but phrased as "don't bring a samovar to Tula."

Russian literature is full of samovars. Writers like Tolstoy and Chekhov used the samovar as a natural backdrop for their scenes — it appears in domestic settings the way a coffee machine might appear in a modern kitchen scene, except with far more emotional and cultural weight.

While the samovar is most closely associated with Russia, it is also deeply embedded in the culture of:

  • Iran — where it is called a samovar as well, and tea is a central part of daily life
  • Turkey — where a similar tea tradition exists
  • Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Armenia, Central Asia, and other parts of the former Soviet Union and surrounding regions
  • Eastern Europe broadly

In all these places, the samovar represents the same thing: a culture that takes tea seriously, drinks it slowly, and treats the making and sharing of tea as a social ritual rather than a quick caffeine fix.

Today, electric samovars are common in homes across Russia, Iran, and Central Asia. They are sold in stores, given as wedding gifts, and proudly displayed in kitchens. Traditional charcoal-fired samovars are still used at outdoor gatherings, picnics, and rural settings where their heat lasts a long time and their presence adds atmosphere.

Antique samovars — especially ornate 19th-century silver or brass ones — are collector's items and can be worth significant amounts of money.
The hostess lit the samovar before the guests arrived so the water would be ready when it was time to serve tea.
The essence of the word, summed up

A samovar is a tall, ornate, metal hot-water urn — traditionally heated by burning charcoal inside a central tube, now often electric — used to keep water hot for extended tea service. It is especially central to Russian culture, where it has been a symbol of hospitality, family life, and warmth for centuries. It sits at the heart of a tea tradition in which strong concentrated tea is brewed separately in a small teapot placed on top of the samovar, and then diluted to taste with the samovar's hot water.
